meta.title: Who really said "Great things are not done by impulse, but by a series of small things brought together"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Van Gogh wrote it in Dutch in an 1882 letter to Theo — but he wrote ‘impulse alone’, and the popular English matches no known translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Great things are not done by impulse, but by a series of small things brought together'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Van Gogh — letter 274 to his brother Theo, 22 October 1882. But the famous English wording drops one word that changes what he meant.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Van Gogh really did write this thought — in Dutch, to his brother Theo from The Hague on Sunday, 22 October 1882 — and the manuscript transcription is public and checkable. But the familiar English sentence matches no translation we could locate, and it quietly drops his qualifier: he wrote that the great does not happen through impulse alone.

source.heading: The letter

docMeta.dd: Letter 274 to Theo van Gogh (old numbering 237)
Dutch — manuscript transcription published by the Van Gogh Museum
Popular English wording: no identified translator

source.excerpt: …en de eersten zijn net de lui om dan als ze er toe komen met wilskracht en nadenken te gaan leven, iets groots te doen. Want het groote geschiedt niet bij impulsie alleen en is een aaneenschakeling van kleine dingen die tot elkaar gebragt zijn.
trail: Van Gogh wrote the sentence in Dutch on Sunday, 22 October 1882, in a letter to his brother Theo — letter 274 in the Van Gogh Museum’s edition, numbered 237 in the older sequence. The museum’s transcription reads “Want het groote geschiedt niet bij impulsie alleen…”, and its authorized English gives “For the great doesn’t happen through impulse alone”: Vincent van Gogh: The Letters, letter 274 ↗.

Quote Investigator ↗ examined the saying and concluded that Van Gogh’s 1882 letter “contained statements matching the two parts of the target quotation,” while cautioning that “different translations into English are possible” and that the two parts “were not immediately adjacent.” The earliest citation QI presents for the popular English wording is a United Press International “Today’s Almanac” column of 30 March 1988.

An older English text of the same letter, hosted at WebExhibits ↗ and credited there to Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, edited by Robert Harrison, renders the phrase as “a succession of small things linked together” — again not the circulating wording.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the saying among Van Gogh’s 1882 quotes, sourced to the 22 October 1882 letter to Theo, alongside a shorter variant: “Great things are done by a series of small things brought together.”
source.excerptNote: The Van Gogh Museum’s authorized English renders the bold sentence as “For the great doesn’t happen through impulse alone, and is a succession of little things that are brought together.” The popular quotation drops alleen (“alone”) and trades “succession of little things” for “series of small things brought together.”

source.rightsNote: Van Gogh’s Dutch original is his own writing from 1882 and is not the problem. The English sentence people actually share is: it corresponds to no translation we could identify, names no translator, and the earliest citation Quote Investigator presents for it is a 1988 newspaper column. The one modern English text that is clearly authorized — the Van Gogh Museum’s 2009 edition of Vincent van Gogh: The Letters — reads differently and is itself in copyright. With the wording’s origin unknown, we assert no public-domain status for it.

author.name: Vincent van Gogh
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: Vincent van Gogh
author.bio: Vincent Willem van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter, born in Zundert on 30 March 1853 and dead by his own hand at Auvers-sur-Oise on 29 July 1890, aged 37. In little more than a decade he produced roughly 2,100 works, the bulk of the paintings in his final two years. He was also a relentless letter-writer: the correspondence with his brother Theo runs to hundreds of letters and is the reason we can check a sentence like this one against a manuscript rather than a meme.

misattribution.heading: What happens to it in transit
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fabrication — it is a loose translation that hardened into a slogan. Three things happen to Van Gogh’s sentence on the way to the poster:

items.who: “by impulse” in place of “by impulse alone”
items.why: Van Gogh’s Dutch is niet bij impulsie alleen — not by impulse alone — and the Van Gogh Museum’s authorized English keeps the word: “For the great doesn’t happen through impulse alone” ↗. Dropping it turns a remark about what is not sufficient into a claim that impulse plays no part at all.

items.who: “And great things are not accidental, but must certainly be willed”
items.why: The saying often circulates as one flowing sentence. Quote Investigator ↗ points out that the two parts “were not immediately adjacent” in the letter — Van Gogh’s passage about drawing and the “invisible iron wall” sits between them — and suggests an ellipsis to mark the gap.

items.who: Nobody — the English has no known source
items.why: The familiar sentence matches neither the Van Gogh Museum’s 2009 translation nor the older English at WebExhibits ↗, which reads “a succession of small things linked together.” The earliest citation Quote Investigator presents for the popular wording is a United Press International “Today’s Almanac” column of 30 March 1988.

misattribution.truthLine: Van Gogh did write it, in Dutch, on 22 October 1882 — but what he wrote is that the great does not happen through impulse alone: letter 274 ↗.

context.heading: Why he was writing about small things
lead: The letter is not a motivational note. Van Gogh is arguing with Theo about people who announce fine principles and never act on them, and he lands on a distinction he cared about: principles are worth something only when they turn into deeds. The line about small things is the hinge of that argument — his point is that a resolve big enough to matter is assembled, not felt.

Then he does something the poster version never shows. He turns immediately to his own craft and asks what drawing actually is, and answers that it is working through an invisible iron wall standing between what you feel and what you can do — a wall you cannot hammer down, only undermine, slowly and patiently. That passage is the small things, described from the inside. It is also, literally, the text that sits between the two halves people now quote as one sentence.
detailsBody: The Van Gogh Museum’s edition carries two numbers for this letter: 274 in the 2009 edition, 237 in the older sequence still used by many reprints and websites. Both refer to the same letter of 22 October 1882.

Van Gogh closes the same passage with the second half of the popular quotation — in the museum’s English, “the great isn’t something accidental; it must be willed” — but only after the drawing digression, which is why Quote Investigator recommends an ellipsis when the two are quoted together.
context.pull: “It’s working one’s way through an invisible iron wall that seems to stand between what one feels and what one can do.”
